review.head: dca522f
review.summary: Blind review found 1 BLOCKER, 0 HIGH, 0 MEDIUM. Three of four focus areas pass; clock propagation has a discarded-parameter mismatch that causes TypeError at runtime.

timeout_mechanism.analysis: TimeoutJobExecutor spawns a child process via multiprocessing. On timeout, proc.terminate()/proc.kill() kills the child. The child holds its own database connection (created inside _run_job_in_child). Signal delivery severs the TCP connection; PostgreSQL rolls back any in-flight transaction. The parent only reaches the kill path when proc.is_alive() is True, meaning the child has NOT committed. If the child had committed, is_alive() returns False and the result is read from the queue. No signal handler in the child to intercept SIGTERM/SIGKILL. Conclusion: a timed-out child cannot commit results — the mechanism is sound.

reaper_atomicity.analysis: StaleRunReaper.recover() calls recover_stale_runs() which finds runs with status='running' and expired leases. _abort_one() then uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the specific run row to gate the abort. Two concurrent reapers would both find the same stale run, but PostgreSQL's row-level lock serializes them: the winner sees status='running' and proceeds; the loser blocks until the winner commits, then sees status != 'running' and returns without double-aborting. The FOR UPDATE lock is the correct atomicity primitive.

shutdown_flag.analysis: OrchestrationWorker._shutdown_flag (threading.Event) is checked at two levels: (1) the main start() loop condition while not self._shutdown_flag.is_set(), and (2) inside _claim_and_execute() before each item in the due list. When stop() sets the flag, the main loop exits and no new claim_due_schedules() calls are made. Any claims already fetched from the database but not yet executed are skipped (break). Crucially, next_run_at is NOT advanced for skipped items (advance happens inside _execute_scheduled which is never reached), so those schedules remain claimable by another worker. The graceful shutdown waits up to GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_SECONDS (30s) for in-flight work to complete.

clock_propagation.finding: create_run and create_attempt called with clock=self._clock but neither function accepts a clock parameter

create_run.signature: create_run(session, *, job_definition_id, schedule_id, idempotency_key, status, triggered_by, scheduled_at, household_id)
create_run.error: TypeError: create_run() got an unexpected keyword argument 'clock'

create_attempt.error: TypeError: create_attempt() got an unexpected keyword argument 'clock'

detail.root_cause: The clock parameter was correctly removed from both functions (it was dead code — create_run uses explicit scheduled_at, and create_attempt doesn't use timestamps). However, the call sites in OrchestrationWorker._execute_scheduled() were not updated to stop passing clock=.
detail.why_tests_pass: Tests never exercise _execute_scheduled: test_worker_stops_claiming_on_shutdown calls worker.stop() BEFORE _claim_and_execute, so the shutdown flag break in the for loop prevents reaching _execute_scheduled. The create_run test calls it directly without clock=. The create_attempt function has no dedicated test.
detail.impact: Any production worker processing a schedule will crash with TypeError on the first job.
